newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia PM defends record ahead of Sunday poll.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM defends record ahead of Sunday poll.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek on Friday toured a depressed northern mining region, hit by Slovenia's drive towards a free market economy, as he ended his month-long campaign for re-election.
Drnovsek spent the morning in Trbovlje, where mine closures have forced the loss of more than 2,000 jobs since independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991.
The hardships in the hilly mining region 70 km (50 miles) east of Ljubljana may have repercussions for Drnovsek, whose constituency lies in the area, in Sunday's general election.
National unemployment is around 13.5 percent but Drnovsek defended his economic record saying Slovenia was regarded as the most successful country among Europe's ex-communist states.

"The difference between Slovenia and comparable countries (former communist states) is huge," Drnovsek told Slovenian television. "Our economic indicators are better than Portugal, Greece and Ireland, who are in the European Union already."
EU membership has been a key platform of Drnvosek's centre-left Liberal Democrats. Ljubljana signed an association pact with the EU in June and expects to join the bloc by 2001.
"By the year 2000, I see Slovenia as a developed country, a full member of NATO which will mean our final step over the threshold into a stable and secure world," Drnovsek said.
Slovenia has emerged as a front-runner with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to be among the first wave of ex-communist states to join the NATO military alliance.
The government received a thumbs-up from financial markets on Friday, with stocks rising partly on confidence that Drnovsek will lead Slovenia's new administration.
"If the Liberal Democrats remain in power, shares will rise significantly next week," said Toni Apollonia, an analyst of Ljubljana's Bank A.
Around 1.5 million Slovenes are eligible to vote in the general election, the second in Slovenia since independence.
But Drnovsek has come under intense criticism from rightist opponents, who have blamed his administration for rising unemployment and an increase in crime.

Rightist parties have set up an informal alliance, calling itself the "Slovenian Spring" to try to wrench the reins of power from Drnovsek, but latest polls show the Liberal Democrats with most support at up to 22 percent.
The "Slovenian Spring" comprises the People's Party, the conservative Christian Democrats and the centre-right Social Democrats.
Opinion polls show combined support for all three parties at around 23 percent with about a third of the electorate still undecided.
